title: Detection of DNS Server
summary: This detection strategy covers acquisition or takeover of domain name system servers, which an adversary uses to control how names resolve for chosen domains or to redirect traffic to attacker controlled infrastructure. Control of a name server lets an attacker move mail, intercept sessions and obtain certificates for names that appear entirely legitimate. The telemetry that makes it visible is authoritative name server query and change logging, registrar or hosting provider audit records, passive resolution history and certificate transparency monitoring. It fails in practice because the change is made through a provider account, so the defender often learns about it from customers rather than from their own monitoring.

beginner.definition: A domain name system server answers the question where does this name point. It is often called a name server. If an attacker controls it, they can send visitors to the wrong place. They can also take over mail for a domain. This detection watches for changes to the name servers that answer for your domains.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most users trust a name, not an address. If the name still looks correct, they will not notice that the traffic goes somewhere else. A name server change can redirect web mail, virtual private network logins and software updates. It can also let an attacker obtain a valid certificate for your name, which defeats certificate warnings. Because the change is made in a provider portal, it may leave no trace in your own network logs. Only provider audit records and independent monitoring can reveal it.
howItWorks: Your domain registrar records every change to the name server entries for your zones.
Your domain name system provider records every record change and the account that made it.
A monitoring service reports new records seen by resolvers around the world.
The detection compares each change with the approved name server list for the domain.
It also watches for certificates issued for names that should only resolve inside your network.
An unapproved name server or a sudden record change raises a high priority alert.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign in sheet at the main reception. Visitors ask for a ward and the receptionist points the way. If somebody replaced the receptionist, every visitor would still arrive somewhere, but not where they expected. The building would look the same and the signs would not change. Only the directions would be wrong. A name server is that receptionist for your domain. Your detection watches the staff roster, so that a replacement is noticed the moment the desk changes hands.
takeaways: Whoever controls your name servers controls where your names point.
The change often happens in a provider portal, far from your own logs.
Independent resolution monitoring is the only way to see it quickly.

objectives: Explain what an authoritative name server does for a domain.
List the provider audit records that show name server changes.
Describe how passive resolution monitoring detects hijacking.
Build an approved list of name servers and registrar contacts.
Plan a response when a name server change is unauthorised.
dataSources: Authoritative name server query and zone change logs with account, source address and record payload
Registrar or domain name system hosting audit records for name server and record update operations
Passive domain name system monitoring results showing resolution changes reported by global resolvers
Certificate transparency logs filtered to names inside your registered domains
Internal list of approved name servers, registrar contacts and change procedures
logic: The pattern is a change to the authoritative name server set or to key records such as mail exchanger and mail authentication records for a domain you own, made outside an approved change. The fields that must be correlated are the zone name, the record type and value, the account that made the change, the source address of that account and the independent resolution results from external monitoring. Benign changes come from planned migrations, provider maintenance and disaster recovery tests announced in advance. The malicious case is an unapproved name server, a shortened record time to live followed by a redirect, or a registration contact change that nobody on the team requested.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Authoritative Name Server Change Outside Approved Maintenance
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection_change:
#     event_type:
#       - 'nameserver_update'
#       - 'zone_record_change'
#   selection_impact:
#     record_type|in:
#       - 'NS'
#       - 'MX'
#       - 'A'
#   filter_approved:
#     account|in: 'approved_dns_pipeline_accounts'
#   filter_window:
#     change_approved: 'true'
#   condition: selection_change and selection_impact and not filter_approved and not filter_window
# level: high
falsePositives: A planned migration to a new domain name system provider carried out under a change ticket.
Provider side maintenance that rotates name server host names inside the same service.
Disaster recovery tests that temporarily point records at a standby site.
A marketing team that adds a new subdomain record without telling the platform team.
tuningNotes: Build the approved name server and record list with the team that owns each domain, and connect it to your change process. Filter the automation accounts that publish records and the maintenance windows agreed with your provider. Scope the alerting rule to name server, mail exchanger and mail authentication records, and report other record changes in a daily summary. If you narrow the rule to name server changes only, you lose the slower takeover that moves a single address record first, so keep a second low severity branch on time to live reductions.
